Shanghai Travel Guide
 Shanghai, which attracts millions of tourists every year, has consistently ranked at the top of China's most popular tourist cities. This makes a lot of people wonder — why is it so appealing? To begin with, as the most modern international metropolis in China, Shanghai boasts the largest number and tallest skyscrapers, as well as the most magnificent night views. A futuristic world constructed by scientific technology is vividly demonstrated here. While Shanghai is more than just modernization. With streets surrounded by luxuriant plane trees and numerous European-style buildings, it still retains the feeling of old Shanghai from a hundred years ago. It is precisely this blend of modernity and retro, Western and Chinese elements that gives this city its greatest charm. European-style Buildings along the Bund 
Besides, by virtue of Shanghai’s well-developed tourism supporting facilities, you will find everything here including transportation, payment, and accommodation very convenient. Moreover, as the third-largest aviation hub in the world, Shanghai has an extensive network of routes connecting to other parts of the globe, making it the first stop for countless overseas tourists when embarking on their journey to China.
AttractionsThe Huangpu River and the Bund are the must-see attractions in Shanghai. Strolling along this river, you will have a strong feeling for the contrast between the modernization and the retro charm of the city. On the east bank stand towering skyscrapers presenting a prosperous urban image, while on the west bank is the Bund with a group of century-old European-style architectures.
Yu Garden, featuring a totally different style from its surroundings, is a hidden gem in the city center. As one of the most representative classical Chinese gardens, it fully showcases the elegance of traditional Chinese architecture. Traveling farther, you will feel the diversity of Shanghai more deeply in Zhujiajiao Ancient Town. Located in the suburbs, it contrasts sharply with the hustle and bustle of the urban area. Here, you can quietly admire the bridges and flowing water and stroll along the cobblestone paths, enjoying the peacefulness of the town. If you are interested in Chinese history and culture, you will be amazed about the comprehensive collection of ancient Chinese art in the Shanghai Museum East.

TransportationShanghai is the most comprehensive transportation hub in China. It boasts extensive international and national air routes, as well as rail routes, so whether you fly directly from overseas, make a flight transfer within China, or take the high-speed train from other Chinese cities, you can smoothly reach Shanghai.
Besides, there are various transportation options for you to travel around Shanghai. Just plan your itinerary in advance and decide which mode of transportation to take. Shanghai Pudong Airport Terminal Shanghai Metro  
How to Get to Shanghai?Shanghai has two major international airports, Hongqiao and Pudong, with routes connecting to 302 destinations in 53 countries around the world. No matter where you depart from – Asia, Europe, Americas, Africa, Oceania, or from any of China’s major cities – you can get to Shanghai successfully. Additionally, the land transportation in Shanghai is well-connected. If you are going to start from any other Chinese cities, such as Beijing, Xi’an, Chongqing, Guangzhou, etc., just a high-speed rail ticket can send you directly to Shanghai.
How to Get Around in Shanghai?The public transportation system within Shanghai is both diverse and intelligent. Metro, bus, and ferry all take turns to serve your travel around the city. Among them, metro is the most recommended transportation tool, as it facilitates your journey by avoiding traffic congestion on the roads. Moreover, the subway lines cover most of the popular attractions and commercial zones in the city, which provides tourists with great convenience. However, during off-peak hours or if you want to visit some scenic spots in the suburbs, then taking a taxi is also an optimal choice. It not only enhances the travel comfort but also allows you to directly reach the destination.

Shanghai Weather & Best Time to Visit
Shanghai has a subtropical monsoon climate and characterized by four distinct seasons. January to February is the coldest period, with the temperature fluctuating between 3 to 5℃ (37 - 41℉). July to August are the hottest months, with temperatures often rising to 40℃ (104℉); and affected by oceanic climate, shanghai tends to be muggy in summer. Besides, there is rainy season in Shanghai that usually falls in mid-June to early July. Your travel experience would be compromised during this time. 
The best times to visit Shanghai are April to May and October to November. During these periods, the weather is balmy, combined with beautiful natural scenery.

Where to Stay in Shanghai?The most recommended areas to stay in Shanghai are locations near the Bund on the west bank of Huangpu River where a lot of popular attractions gather around. Also, these places feature well-connected transportation networks, providing great convenience for your trip. Furthermore, there are diverse hotels to pick, ranging from mid-range to high-end. Just standing by the hotel window, you can enjoy an enchanting night view of the Bund. However, the accommodation expenses in these areas are relatively high.
If you want to stay in a more cost-effective hotel, then locations near all the subway stations on the west bank of Huangpu River are suitable. Additionally, if you are a business traveler, then living in places on the east bank would be ideal since major conference centers are located here.
How Long to Stay in Shanghai?Tourists with a tight schedule can generally complete an itinerary in 2 - 3 days by visiting core landmarks such as the Bund, Yu Garden, Lujiazui, and Nanjing Road. If you are interested in Chinese history and culture, it’s recommended to spend an extra day to visit the Shanghai Museum East and explore the Shikumen buildings of Tianzifang. Anyway, it’s not possible to fully explore Shanghai in just one short journey since its diverse landscapes are scattered at every corner of the city. Yet regardless of how much time you spend here, you’ll always gain a precious travel memory.
Shanghai Food Shanghai Food: Pan-fried Pork Bun Shanghai local cuisine offers a balanced flavor of sweetness and saltiness. Braised pork is one of the most representative Shanghai dishes. Having been simmered slowly over a long time, the fatty part of the pork has become velvety so it melts in your mouth immediately, while the lean part has become very tender. Other than that, Shanghai local snacks are worth trying, too. Taking a bite of pan-fried pork bun with thin wrapper and crispy bottom, you can taste the delicious meat filling with rich gravy. The butterfly pastry, with a rich butter aroma, has a soft texture and just right sweet flavor.
Above all, Shanghai is a melting pot of cuisines from all over China, meaning you are able to enjoy various authentic dishes of other Chinese cities without stepping out of this city, such as Xi’an Chinese hamburger, Beijing fried sauce noodles, Chongqing hotpot, etc. Also, Shanghai is rich in coffee culture, with the largest number of coffee shops across the country. It would be very nice to enjoy a quiet coffee time while strolling around the city.
ShoppingApart from visiting popular attractions, shopping is another main purpose for many tourists to come to Shanghai. Numerous large shopping zones gather here enticing shoppers from home and abroad. Nanjing Road, as the top commercial street in China, houses almost all the types of goods you want, including trendy clothing designed by emerging designers, high-end custom-made suits and cheongsams, as well as electronic products like drones and mobile phones. In addition, many tax refund shops are scattered around the city, enabling you to enjoy Instant Tax Refund service in the store after buying the souvenirs. Shanghai Nanjing Road Tourists Shopping in the Store  
NightlifeShanghai is renowned as the “Everbright City”. The night view of the Bund, together with that of Hong Kong’s Victoria Harbor, is regarded as one of the most beautiful nightscapes in Asia. When the night falls, ripples of the Huangpu River shine brilliantly with tenderness as neon lights illuminate the magnificent architecture of the Bund and the grand buildings on the opposite. Taking a cruise is the best way to enjoy such beautiful view. Just in one hour, you will be able to fully appreciate the panoramic night views of both banks.
Throughout the city, there are numerous commercial streets, restaurants and various bars that remain open until late at night.  Night View of the Huangpu River

title: 陆家嘴 - 上海金融中心摩天大楼天际线 - LoongWander
text:
陆家嘴位于上海市浦东新区黄浦江畔，是上海的金融中心与地标性文旅集聚区。陆家嘴地理范围东至浦东南路、环路，南至东昌路，西、北临黄浦江，总面积约1.7平方公里。作为上海浦东开发开放的核心地标，陆家嘴以密集的超高层建筑群、完善的金融服务体系和独特的滨江景观为核心特色，拥有多座高度位列全球前列的摩天大楼，其中上海中心大厦总高度632米，为中国第一、世界第三高楼；上海环球金融中心高度492米，金茂大厦高度420.5米，三座建筑共同构成“陆家嘴三件套”城市天际线。截至2025年，陆家嘴区域集聚了超千家金融机构、数十家跨国公司地区总部，同时融合了滨江休闲、都市观光、文化体验等多元旅游功能，年接待游客超千万人次，是上海都市旅游的核心名片。
历史文化
陆家嘴的名称源于明代翰林院学士陆深，其家族曾在此聚居，且此地位于黄浦江转弯处，形似“嘴”状，故而得名。在近代，陆家嘴曾是上海的轻工业聚集地和码头仓储区，见证了上海近代工业的起步与发展，留存有少量近代工业建筑遗迹，成为浦东历史脉络的重要佐证。
1990年，上海浦东开发开放战略正式启动，陆家嘴被确立为国家级金融贸易区，自此开启了从传统工业区向国际金融中心的转型之路。三十余年间，陆家嘴从一片农田与旧厂房区域，逐步建成集金融、贸易、旅游、文化于一体的现代化城区，其发展历程成为中国改革开放的生动缩影，也形成了“敢闯敢试、敢为人先”的浦东精神，成为陆家嘴独特的文化内核。
如今，陆家嘴在保留金融核心功能的同时，不断融入海派文化与现代都市文化，滨江大道的城市公共空间、各类艺术展馆、文化展演活动等，让陆家嘴不仅是金融高地，更是上海文化交流的重要平台，实现了经济与文化的双向赋能。
主要景点
上海中心大厦
上海中心大厦坐落于陆家嘴银城中路501号，总建筑面积57.8万平方米，建筑总高度632米，由美国Gensler建筑设计事务所设计，2016年正式投入使用。大厦共118层（地上），地下5层，集办公、酒店、观光、商业等功能于一体，其顶部的“上海之巅”观光厅位于118-119层，海拔546米，配备全球最快的超高速电梯（速度达18米/秒），仅需55秒即可从地下1层抵达观光层，游客可360度俯瞰上海全景，是陆家嘴登高观光的核心景点。
上海中心大厦
上海环球金融中心
上海环球金融中心位于陆家嘴世纪大道100号，建筑高度492米，地上101层，地下3层，总建筑面积38.16万平方米，2008年正式开业。其最具标志性的设计是顶部的“风洞”造型，94层（423米）、97层（439米）和100层（474米）设有观光设施，其中100层的悬空观光长廊采用透明玻璃地面，游客可直面脚下的城市景观，是陆家嘴极具特色的高空观光体验点，大厦同时承载国际金融办公、商业配套等功能。
上海环球金融中心
金茂大厦
金茂大厦位于陆家嘴世纪大道88号，总高度420.5米，地上88层，地下3层，总建筑面积29万平方米，1999年建成开业，是陆家嘴早期的超高层地标建筑。大厦融合了中国传统宝塔建筑风格与现代摩天楼设计，88层观光厅高度340.1米，拥有开放式的高空观景平台，可近距离观赏黄浦江两岸风光；大厦内还设有金茂君悦大酒店，占据53至87层，是世界上最高的酒店之一，成为商务与观光结合的典范。
金茂大厦
陆家嘴滨江大道
陆家嘴滨江大道西起东昌路渡口，东至浦东南路，全长约2.5公里，占地面积约10万平方米，是集休闲、观光、生态于一体的城市滨江公共空间。滨江大道紧邻黄浦江，与外滩万国建筑博览群隔江相望，沿途设置了亲水平台、观景步道、绿化景观带及各类休闲设施，游客可步行欣赏黄浦江景与陆家嘴天际线，也是拍摄上海城市景观的热门地点，每日开放时间为全天，是陆家嘴市民与游客休闲的核心区域。
陆家嘴滨江大道
上海海洋水族馆
上海海洋水族馆位于陆家嘴环路1388号，总建筑面积约20500平方米，是国家AAAA级旅游景区，2002年正式对外开放。馆内拥有长达155米的海底隧道，为世界最长的海底观光隧道之一，展示了来自全球五大洲、四大洋的超500种、超10000尾水生生物，包括中华鲟、扬子鳄等珍稀物种，是集展示、科普、教育于一体的海洋主题展馆，年接待游客超200万人次。
上海海洋水族馆
上海迪士尼旗舰店
上海迪士尼旗舰店（陆家嘴店）位于陆家嘴丰和路180号，是迪士尼在中国大陆的首家旗舰店，建筑面积约5000平方米，店内汇集了迪士尼全系列主题商品，从经典卡通形象周边到限量版纪念品，是亲子游玩与迪士尼粉丝打卡的热门地点，同时建筑外观融入迪士尼经典元素，成为陆家嘴商业文旅的特色节点。
上海迪士尼旗舰店
游玩路线
推荐陆家嘴一日经典游玩路线：上午9:00抵达陆家嘴地铁站（2号线），首先前往上海海洋水族馆（游玩约2小时），近距离观赏海洋生物；11:30前往滨江大道，沿黄浦江步行至东昌路渡口段，欣赏外滩与陆家嘴天际线，途中可在滨江休闲区稍作休息，享用简餐；下午13:30前往金茂大厦88层观光厅（游玩约1小时），体验高空观景；15:00前往上海环球金融中心，打卡100层悬空观光长廊（游玩约1.5小时）；16:30前往上海中心大厦，登顶“上海之巅”观光厅（游玩约1小时），欣赏日落时分的上海全景；18:00后可前往陆家嘴中心L+Mall或正大广场享用晚餐，餐后可在滨江大道观赏外滩夜景，结束当日行程。若时间充裕，可增加迪士尼旗舰店、陆家嘴中心绿地等点位，调整为两日游玩路线，首日侧重高空观光与滨江景观，次日侧重海洋馆与商业体验。
游玩建议
最佳游玩时间：春秋两季（3-5月、9-11月），气温适宜，能见度高，适合登高观景；若想观赏夜景，建议选择周五、周六晚间，外滩及陆家嘴灯光秀效果更佳，灯光开放时间为18:00-22:30。
登高观光建议：上海中心大厦、环球金融中心、金茂大厦任选1-2座即可，避免重复体验；建议提前1-2天在官方平台购票，可节省现场排队时间。
亲子游玩建议：优先选择上海海洋水族馆+迪士尼旗舰店的组合，海洋水族馆建议游玩时长2-3小时，避开周末及节假日高峰，每日9:00开馆时入场人流量较少。
摄影建议：拍摄陆家嘴天际线最佳点位为滨江大道东昌路渡口附近，拍摄外滩与陆家嘴同框最佳时间为日落前1小时（“黄金时刻”）；拍摄高空全景建议携带广角镜头，上海中心118层观光厅允许使用非专业摄影设备。
餐饮建议：陆家嘴区域餐饮价格偏高，可选择正大广场、陆家嘴中心L+Mall等综合商场就餐，滨江区域也有简餐咖啡店。
游玩时长：核心景点全覆盖建议1天（8小时），若包含深度体验（如酒店下午茶、展馆细逛）建议1.5-2天。
注意事项
登高观光注意：上海中心、环球金融中心、金茂大厦的观光厅均禁止携带易燃易爆物品、大件行李（超过20寸行李箱），玻璃栈道区域禁止穿高跟鞋踩踏，儿童需由成人陪同，1.2米以下儿童部分场馆免票。
人流管控：节假日（如春节、国庆）陆家嘴核心区域会实施人流管控，部分路段可能临时封闭，建议提前关注浦东新区文旅局公告，错峰出行。
交通提示：陆家嘴地铁站（2号线）节假日高峰时段会限流，建议选择14号线浦东南路站、9号线商城路站出站后步行前往，避免拥堵。
天气提示：登高观景受天气影响较大，若遇雾霾、大雨天气，能见度会大幅降低，建议出行前查询空气质量指数（AQI），AQI低于100时观景效果最佳。
财物安全：陆家嘴游客密集区域，需注意保管手机、钱包等随身物品，滨江大道等开阔区域谨防无人机、风筝等高空物品坠落风险。
设施使用：滨江大道的公共座椅、卫生间等设施免费使用，禁止占用公共空间摆摊、露营，遵守公共场所管理规定。
交通
地铁：乘坐上海地铁2号线至陆家嘴站（1号、2号、6号口出站均可直达核心区域）；14号线至浦东南路站（4号口出站，步行约800米至滨江大道）；9号线至商城路站（1号口出站，步行约1公里至陆家嘴中心区域）。
公交：陆家嘴区域公交线路有81路、82路、583路、799路、939路、961路等，陆家嘴环路丰和路站、陆家嘴地铁站站为核心公交站点，可直达各景点。
轮渡：从浦西外滩金陵东路渡口乘坐东金线轮渡至东昌路渡口，渡江约10分钟，上岸后步行5分钟即可到达滨江大道，是体验黄浦江交通的特色方式。
自驾：陆家嘴核心区域停车场主要有正大广场停车场、上海中心大厦停车场、金茂大厦停车场，节假日停车位紧张，建议优先选择公共交通。
出租车/网约车：陆家嘴区域网约车下车点主要集中在正大广场南门、上海中心大厦东门、滨江大道东昌路入口处，禁止在主干道随意停车上下客。

title: The Former French Concession, Shanghai: Is It Worth Visiting
text:

The Former French Concession, Shanghai: Is It Worth Visiting？
We will say yes, if you want to experience Shanghai beyond the postcard skyline. And, no, if you only want famous landmarks.
The Former French Concession is a large historic area, worth about 1–2 hours on a first trip, especially if you enjoy walking around slowly for architecture, cafés, and seeing how old Shanghai still fits into everyday city life.
To see the Former French Concession, pick one compact neighborhood, take your time strolling around, and stop when the experience feels complete.
For most first-time visitors, the best choice is Wukang Road → Anfu Road.
What's Actually Worth Your Time?
Choose Your FFC Route That Suits Your Time
When Is the Best Time to Visit
FAQs
What Is Actually Worth Seeing in the Former French Concession?
For a 1–2 hour walk, choose one or two roads and a commercial area for a complete atmospheric experience.
Wukang Road: A Must for First-timers
Wukang Road
This is where you should come for the classic Former French Concession look.
Walk slowly, and look up from time to time. The best part is the sequence of plane trees, villas, apartment buildings, balconies, and quiet residential lanes.
Wukang Mansion is the visual landmark, but the surrounding streets are what make the area worth walking.
Anfu Road: Best for Cafés and Modern Shanghai
Anfu Road direction sign board
Anfu Road gives you the other half of the experience.
Come here when you want to stop for coffee, browse small shops, or watch the street become busier around lunchtime.
This is where the Former French Concession feels most like a living neighborhood rather than an architectural open-air museum.
Fuxing Road: Best for a Quieter Walk
Fuxing Park at Fuxing Road
Turn toward Fuxing Road for less touristy stops.
You will see more residential lanes and fewer commercial storefronts.
This is the side to choose when your idea of sightseeing is simply walking, looking around, and slowing down.
Xintiandi: Worth Combining, Not Worth Forcing Into a Short Walk
Lanes of Shanghai Xintiandi
Xintiandi is polished, commercial, and redeveloped. 
It keeps traditional Shikumen architecture, and is useful when you want restaurants, shopping, air-conditioning, or a more comfortable break.
But it should not replace the street-level experience of Wukang Road and Anfu Road.
And do not assume it is next door: Wukang Road and Xintiandi are about 4 km apart.
Tianzifang: A Maze of Lilongs, Skippable if You Are Short on Time
Shanghai Tianzifang
Tianzifang still preserves the authentic lilong life, and walking into it, a maze of narrow alleyways packed with small shops, still gives you the feeling of stepping back into the 20th century.
Although it has declined somewhat, it is still very lively on holidays and weekends.
Worth a look if you enjoy quirky shopping and don't mind the bustle; skip if you want space, quiet, or are on a tight schedule.
6-Day Beijing and Shanghai Tour A Tale of Two Cities 
Choose Your FFC Route That Suits Your Time
The Former French Concession Map
1–2 Hours: Wukang Road → Anfu Road
This is our recommended first-time route. It gives you enough time to appreciate the architecture without turning the visit into a checklist.
Start around Wukang Road. You will walk through the historic residential streets, pause for photos, and continue north toward Anfu Road.
Allow 20–30 minutes for a coffee or bakery stop rather than trying to squeeze in another major attraction.
You will finish with the part of the district that feels most alive: shops opening, people meeting friends, and cafés spilling onto the street.
If you have more time to explore, you can take a taxi to Xintiandi or Tianzifang to see the clever integration of historical buildings and modern commercial spaces.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
3 Hours or More: Consider a Historic Themed Route for a Deeper Dive
If you're looking for more than a pleasant walk, this route introduces you to the district's hidden history.
Your walk will be guided from Fuxing Park and Sinan Mansions to Donghu Hotel, and end at the Wukang Mansion, following the life of Du Yuesheng, Shanghai's most infamous gangster-turned-power-broker, to show you a different side of the district.
Passing by today's peaceful architecture, it is hard to imagine that behind it lie bloody suppression, armed clashes, and layers of power, ambition, and memory.
Less Than 1 Hour: Wukang Road + Xintiandi
It is a taste of the Former French Concession, not a full visit.
With less than 1 hour, just tick off Wukang Mansion, look at the villas and plane trees, take your photos, and leave. Then you can take a taxi straight to Xintiandi for a short stroll, or simply end here.
Do not try to walk to Xintiandi from Wukang Road.
Wukang Road to Xintiandi is about 4.2 km on foot, so walking between the two takes roughly 50 minutes.
When Is the Best Time to Visit FFC?
8:30–10:00 AM: Best for Local Life and Quiet Streets
Morning on Wukang Road, Shanghai
This is our top choice for a first visit.
Start around 8:30 or 9:00 AM if you want quieter streets and a stronger sense of the neighborhood before the sightseeing crowds build.
You may see residents walking dogs, people picking up breakfast, and office workers moving through the streets.
You also get the advantage of cooler temperatures, which matters on hot Shanghai days.
2:00–4:30 PM: Best for Cafés and a Slow Afternoon
Find a café for a rest on Anfu Road
Choose the afternoon when you care more about cafés, shops, and a relaxed pace.
Take a walk for about an hour. Stop for coffee. Then continue exploring the streets.
This works particularly well when you target the Former French Concession as your slower afternoon experience, rather than the first attraction of the day.
After Sunset: Skip It for Architecture
Night view of Wukang Road, Shanghai
Do not come here at night specifically to "see the Former French Concession."
Once it gets dark, you lose much of what makes the area special: the building designs, balconies, plane-tree canopy, and residential streetscape.
Come in the evening only when you have a specific restaurant, bar, or dinner reservation in mind.
9-Day Beijing ,Xian and Shanghai Tour China Family Classic Tour 
FAQs About the Former French Concession
Can You Go Inside the Old Houses?
Former Residence of Zhou Enlai (Shanghai)
Usually, no. Most historic residences are still private homes, offices, or other working buildings.
You can walk along the streets, photograph exteriors, and look into public lane entrances, but you should not treat historic residences as open museums.
For an interior experience, we will choose several buildings that officially admit visitors, such as the Soong Ching-ling Memorial Residence and Xuhui Old Houses Art Center.
Instead of repeatedly wondering which buildings you can enter, you can focus on the streets and let the guide do the reservations and explain what you are seeing.
Is It Worth Visiting With Kids or Senior Travelers?
Yes, but do not turn it into a long-distance walking tour.
For families, the 1–2-hour Wukang Road → Anfu Road route is the better choice.
You can stop for drinks, coffee, food, or a break whenever needed.
The experience also works well for teenagers because it combines architecture with cafés, shops, photography, and ordinary Shanghai street life rather than requiring them to spend hours inside museums.
Traveling with children or older family members? We can keep the walking route compact and add vehicle transfers so you experience the neighborhood without exhausting everyone.
What should I combine with the Former French Concession?
Our guests had a good time at the Bund
The Former French Concession pairs well with several other Shanghai experiences, depending on your interests and how much time you have.
The Bund: This is the most popular combination. Spend the morning or afternoon in the French Concession, then head to the Bund for sunset. Seeing both in one day gives you a well-rounded sense of the city, and split it into two days if you want a deeper connection to the Bund.
Jing'an Temple or Jade Buddha Temple: A good pairing if you want a contrast between historic urban fabric and traditional Buddhist architecture. 
M50 Creative Park: If you're interested in contemporary art, M50 offers gallery spaces inside converted factory buildings, great for art lovers hopping between free exhibitions and artworks.

title: Zhujiajiao Water Town: How to See Its Less Touristy Side
text:
Home

Zhujiajiao Water Town: How to See Its Less Touristy Side
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 10, 2026 
If you have only 1–2 days in Shanghai, skip Zhujiajiao and focus on the Bund, Yu Garden, the Former French Concession, and the city's skyline.
But if you have 3 days or more, Zhujiajiao is worth a half-day, especially if you want a slower contrast to central Shanghai.
The trick is to avoid spending your whole visit on the main canal streets. Give yourself 3–4 hours to mix residential lanes, old gardens, stone bridges, and quiet canal views.
Is Zhujiajiao Worth Half a Day?
Zhujiajiao Less-touristy Route
Should You Take a Boat in Zhujiajiao?
Is Zhujiajiao Suitable for Children and Older Travelers?
When Is the Best Time to Visit Zhujiajiao
How to Get to Zhujiajiao
Is Zhujiajiao Worth Half a Day?
Zhujiajiao Water Town in summer season
Our picks:
1–2 days in Shanghai: Skip Zhujiajiao.
3 days: Optional. Go if you have already covered the main sights and want a slower half-day outside central Shanghai.
4+ days: Recommended. You have enough time to add Zhujiajiao without taking time away from Shanghai's major sights.
Yes, Zhujiajiao is a real historic town. If you want to experience a Jiangnan water town without leaving Shanghai for a full day, this is it.
However, it is not an untouched village. The main streets have souvenir shops, snack stalls, restaurants, boat rides, and plenty of visitors. That means your experience depends heavily on when you arrive and where you walk.
If you arrive on a weekday around 8:30–9:00 AM, you can start with quieter residential lanes before the busiest part of the town fills up.
If you only have one full day in Shanghai, this journey to the western suburbs is not the best use of your time.
Unsure whether Zhujiajiao fits your Shanghai itinerary? We can help you compare it with Suzhou, Hangzhou, or another water town before you give up half a day of your trip.
The Best Zhujiajiao Half-Day Route: See the Town, Not Just the Tourist Street
Route: Visitor Center → West Well Street (西井街) → Kezhi Garden (课植园) & Hexin Garden (和心园) → Fangsheng Bridge (放生桥) → Jiangnan First Tea House (江南第一茶楼) → Tai'an Bridge (泰安桥) → Lang Bridge (廊桥) → City God Temple (城隍庙) → Daqing Post Office (大清邮局)
Distance: Roughly 4–5 km (around 7,000–9,000 steps)
Time needed: About 3–4 hours at a relaxed pace
Don't try to turn it into a checklist. The quieter lanes between the landmarks are part of the experience, rather than being hurried from one crowded photo spot to another.
1. Start at West Well Street, Not Fangsheng Bridge
Alleys of the Zhujiajiao Water Town, Shanghai
When you arrive at the visitor center, don't immediately follow the crowd toward the main canal and Fangsheng Bridge.
Turn into West Well Street (西井街) first.
The atmosphere changes quickly. Instead of souvenir shops and tour groups, you'll see residential lanes, older houses, local shops, and people going about their daily routines.
If you have another 30–45 minutes, continue toward East Well Street (东井街). It is a useful extension when you want more residential scenery rather than another landmark.
2. Don't Skip the Gardens: Both Are Worth Visiting
Kezhi Garde in Zhujiajiao Water Town
The canals and bridges show you the postcard side of the town. Kezhi Garden and Hexin Garden show you how wealthy local families actually lived and how Jiangnan garden design worked. They are also a good way to step away from the busiest commercial streets.
Current prices are:
Kezhi Garden: ¥20
Hexin Garden: ¥30
Shanghai Helong Art Gallery: ¥20
Three-attraction joint ticket: ¥60
Kezhi Garden (课植园) is the larger of the two, with more space to explore and a mix of traditional Jiangnan garden design and Western-style architectural elements.
Hexin Garden (和心园) is smaller but more intimate, with its own gardens, historic buildings, and collections.
We recommend both rather than choosing between them. They are different enough that visiting one does not make the other feel repetitive, and together they give you a much better sense of Zhujiajiao beyond its canals and tourist streets.
The paid attractions are open 8:30 AM–5:00 PM. If you buy the ¥60 joint ticket online, you need to exchange it for a physical ticket by 3:00 PM.
For this route, visit the gardens before Fangsheng Bridge. That way, you see the quieter historic side first and leave the busiest canal area for the classic views later.
3. Walk to Fangsheng Bridge for the Classic Zhujiajiao View
Fangsheng Bridge in Zhujiajiao Water Town
Now head toward Fangsheng Bridge (放生桥).
Built in 1571, it is one of Zhujiajiao's defining landmarks and the town's classic viewpoint over the canal.
This is where the water-town image you've probably seen online starts to make sense: stone bridge, whitewashed houses, narrow waterways, willow trees, and wooden boats moving below.
Expect this area to be considerably busier than the residential lanes, which is totally acceptable.
You don't come here to avoid people completely—you come here for the view.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
4. Stop at Jiangnan First Tea House
The Jiangnan First Tea House
After roughly 1½–2 hours of walking, take a proper break.
The Jiangnan First Tea House (江南第一茶楼) sits beside the water and makes a useful 20–30 minute pause.
Order tea, sit by the canal, and watch the boats rather than rushing straight to the next attraction.
This is one of the moments when Zhujiajiao works best: you stop sightseeing and simply watch the town move around you.
5. Cross Tai'an Bridge and Lang Bridge
Lang Bridge in Zhujiajiao Water Town
Continue toward Tai'an Bridge (泰安桥) and then Lang Bridge (廊桥).
Tai'an Bridge is where you'll find the large characters "朱家角" (Zhujiajiao) painted on a wall—the classic spot that signals you've arrived. 
Lang Bridge is a particularly good photo stop because you can frame the canal, old buildings, stone bridges, and wooden boats in one view.
If photography matters to you, this section is more rewarding than trying to collect every bridge in town.
6. Finish at City God Temple and Daqing Post Office
City God Temple in Zhujiajiao Water Town
The City God Temple (城隍庙) is a small stop rather than a major attraction. Give it 10–15 minutes if you enjoy historic religious architecture and quieter courtyards.
Then continue to Daqing Post Office (大清邮局).
This restored Qing-era post office is an easy final stop. You can buy a postcard, have it stamped with a Zhujiajiao postmark, and continue walking without adding much time to your route.
Should You Take a Boat: Treat It as an Add-On, Not a Must
Taking a boat tour at Zhujiajiao Water Town
Our recommendation:
Solo/couple: Walk first; add a boat only if the water experience is important to you.
Family/group of 4–6: A private hand-rowed boat makes more sense.
Already/plan to visit Suzhou/Hangzhou/Guilin: The walking route may give you more variety than another short water-town boat ride.
The boat ride is not a bad experience. It is simply not essential for everyone.
The current official hand-rowed boat routes cost ¥200–300 per boat, with a maximum of 6 passengers, and take about 15–20 minutes.
For a family or group of up to six, the price becomes much easier to justify because you are paying by boat rather than per person.
For a solo traveler or couple, it is a different calculation. It depends on whether you want to charter the boat alone or share it with others.
Instead of spending hours lining up for a 15-minute experience, you may get more value from standing on Fangsheng Bridge or Lang Bridge, where you can see the boats, canals, bridges, and old houses together rather than viewing the scenery from inside a short boat ride.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
Is Zhujiajiao Suitable for Children and Older Travelers?
Yes, with one important warning: the streets are mostly manageable, but the stone bridges can be steep and uneven.
For a slower family visit, stay mainly around: West Well Street → central canal → Fangsheng Bridge → tea house
You do not need to climb every bridge or visit every attraction. For older travelers or anyone with limited mobility, a private transfer can also remove the unnecessary walking between the metro station and the old town.
If you're traveling with children or older family members, we can adjust the route to reduce unnecessary walking while keeping the most photogenic canal and bridge views.
When Is the Best Time to Visit Zhujiajiao: Weekday Morning Beats Weekend Crowds
For the best chance of a quieter experience, arrive around 8:30–9:00 AM on a weekday.
Start with West Well Street and the residential lanes while the town is still relatively calm.
By late morning, the main tourist streets become noticeably busier, particularly on weekends and public holidays.
If you cannot arrive in the morning, arriving after 3:00 PM can give you quieter streets and a different atmosphere. 
But there is a trade-off: the paid attractions close around 5:00 PM, and you may not have enough time to see them all. So a late arrival is better for atmosphere than for sightseeing.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
How to Get to Zhujiajiao: Metro for Value, Private Transfer for Comfort
Metro Line 17: Best for budget travelers. Take Metro Line 17 to Zhujiajiao Station, and use the local scenic shuttle to the visitor center, or walk toward the old town.
Taxi or ride-hailing: Easier for small groups. This is more convenient when you are traveling with children, luggage, or several people. You avoid the transfer from the metro station and arrive closer to the old town.
Private transfer: Best when Zhujiajiao is part of a full Shanghai day. A private transfer becomes worthwhile when you want to combine Zhujiajiao with another Shanghai experience.
Private transfer is particularly useful for families or older travelers who would rather spend their limited sightseeing time walking through Zhujiajiao than navigating public transport.
If you don't want to spend part of your Shanghai day figuring out transfers, we can arrange a private tour and fit Zhujiajiao into your existing Shanghai itinerary.

title: Top Things to Do in Shanghai: Beyond the Landmarks
text:

Top Things to Do in Shanghai: Beyond the Landmarks
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Aug. 6, 2026 
For first-time visitors, if you only have two or three days in Shanghai, don't try to fit in every famous attraction, but know which experiences are actually worth your time.
Instead of planning Shanghai by the number of places you visit, plan it by experiencing the city's different faces.
Imagine yourself walking through streets shaped by history, tasting flavors that have been part of the city for generations, and ending the day watching the lights from the famous Pudong Skyline.
These moments show why Shanghai is not just another modern metropolis, but one of the most memorable stops on a China journey.
This guide is organised by experiences rather than by attraction popularity, helping you balance Shanghai's historic charm, local life, and futuristic energy without wasting hours on places that may not match your expectations.
What's Actually Worth Your Time in Shanghai
Top Things to Do in Shanghai
How to Prioritize If You Have 1, 2, or 3 Days
FAQs
How to Decide What's Actually Worth Your Time in Shanghai
Shanghai has more attractions and experiences than you could possibly fit into one trip. 
If your time is limited, don't try to check off every famous landmark. Instead, prioritize experiences that help you understand what makes Shanghai unique.
We believe the three experiences most worth your time are its history, its everyday life, and its vision of the future. Together, they show you where Shanghai came from, how it lives today, and where it is heading next.
1. Step Into Shanghai's History, Not Just Its Landmarks
The Bund at night
Shanghai's historic neighborhoods are worth your time because they show you how the city's past still shapes its modern identity. 
Instead of simply ticking off historic buildings as sightseeing stops, walk through neighborhoods where the past is still part of everyday life. 
Old residences sit alongside cafés, local shops, and modern businesses, giving you a chance to experience how Shanghai has evolved without leaving its history behind.
2. Experience How Shanghai Actually Lives
Shanghai local farmers market
To truly experience Shanghai, you don't travel all this way to see how it performs for tourists, but to delve into the city locals actually live in. 
From food and morning markets to neighborhood streets and ordinary daily routines, these experiences help you understand the rhythm, character, and energy of Shanghai in a way that famous attractions alone cannot.
What makes its neighborhoods so special is that none of them feels preserved for tourists; it simply feels lived in.
3. See Shanghai's Leap from Past to Future
Pick up a food delivery brought by a drone.
Shanghai's skyline is worth your time because few places make the city's transformation so visible, both from above and on the river. 
In a single view, you can see the contrast between its historic roots and its futuristic ambitions, giving you a sense of how dramatically the city has changed and how fast it is moving forward.
7-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Top Things to Do in Shanghai (Ranked by Experience Value)
Instead of ranking these experiences by how famous the landmarks are, we have ordered them by something more meaningful: the depth of what you actually take away to carry home from each one.
But if you have to pick just two or three, start at the top and work your way down.
1. Walk Along the Bund: See Shanghai's Past and Future Face Each Other
The famous Shanghai skyline
If there is one single spot that justifies the phrase "Shanghai," it is the Bund.  
To get the full effect, the skyline is at its best between 6 PM and 8 PM, when the fading daylight softens the horizon and the new towers begin to sparkle one by one.
Evening is when you will witness the entire riverbank transform into a glowing runway, and the "wow" will remind you why this spot tops our list. But if you want fewer crowds, arrive 30–40 minutes before sunset and stay until the lights come on.
For those who want to explore the Bund in-depth, we recommend a walking tour by day. 
Our guide will walk you through the history of the row of buildings that blend European and Chinese architectural styles and how they survived the war, such as Astor House Hotel, Peace Hotel, and the former HSBC Building.
We are not trying to give you a history lesson, but a chance to see that Shanghai did not erase its past to become modern: it simply built the new by rooting around the old.
If you want to see more aspects of the Bund besides the classic one, combine your Bund walk with a stroll through Waibaidu Bridge to North Bund Green Land, where you find significantly fewer people, unobstructed skyline views, and rewarding scenery along the way.
2. Explore the Former French Concession: Shanghai's Most Walkable Historic Area
The Former French Concession in Shanghai
For visitors who wonder whether Shanghai is nothing but concrete and glass, the Former French Concession tells a different story.
The Former French Concession is at its most lively on weekday mornings (before 9 AM). You'll see locals buying breakfast, walking dogs, opening neighborhood shops, and daily life unfolding beneath the shade of leafy, towering plane trees over quiet, winding streets.
As you wander, keep your eyes open for the old villas with red ceramic roofs and black iron balconies, where elderly residents play chess on folding tables along the streets.
The narrow lilong lanes lead you to hidden courtyards and the tiny cafés that have set up shop in them. Young white-collar workers can always find these quiet hidden gems, enjoy a serene space sipping coffee while tapping on laptops.
If you'd like to explore these quieter lanes without worrying about navigation, our private walking experience combines local food stops with the neighborhood stories most visitors miss.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
3. Taste Shanghai Through Time-Honored Food and Local Flavors
Shanghai Old Restaurant, one of the most famous local cuisine restaurants in Shanghai.
When you start wondering what you should eat in Shanghai, the real question is often: "What will help me understand this city through its flavors?" Embarking on a Shanghai Benbang food adventure may give you the answer.
Our local food walks focus on carefully selected century-old restaurants still loved by Shanghai locals, rather than tourist-only stops. From Dexingguan and Lao Zheng Xing to other historic eateries, you'll taste each restaurant's signature dish and discover the classic flavors that generations of Shanghai diners have enjoyed.
Feel free to inform your tour guide of your dietary restrictions and allergies in advance so they can make further recommendations. 
However, these famed restaurants generally require you to take a number and wait in line, so it's best to arrive as early as possible during peak meal times to minimize the chance of queuing, such as around 11:00 AM or 5:00 PM.
Want to learn how to cook so you can recreate its delicious flavors at home? Travel with China Highlights, and we'll take you from buying ingredients at a local Shanghai market to visiting a local resident's home in a lilong alley, where you'll quickly learn how to make easy and delicious dishes in a cooking class.
4. See Shanghai from Above: Choose One Skyscraper Experience
Enjoy a panoramic view of Shanghai from the observation deck of the Shanghai Tower.
The city offers multiple observation decks on the skyscrapers, and the choice can easily become overwhelming.
Our advice is simple: if this is your first time in Shanghai, just pick the Shanghai Tower and be done with it.
As the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world, it gives you the ultimate advantage of looking down on its two famous neighbors—the Oriental Pearl Tower and the Jin Mao Tower—rather than looking up at them from ground level.
The elevator ride to the 118th floor is an experience in itself, and the 360-degree views from the top give you a comprehensive understanding of Shanghai's urban layout.
If watching the sunset above is a must for you, it's recommended that you arrive around 4 PM to avoid long queues that could delay your trip.
For a romantic night, we can help you reserve a dinner on the 119th floor around 6 PM, where you can witness the city light up after the stunning sunset with your loved one.
5. Cruise Huangpu River at Night: See the City Change After Dark
Shanghai Huangpu River Night Cruise
Shanghai feels busy and businesslike during the day, but takes on a completely different personality once the lights come up: more glamorous, more mysterious, and undeniably more romantic.
You can tell the night version of Shanghai feels like a different city altogether. 
As we mentioned, besides taking an evening walk along the Bund and having a romantic dinner on the top of the Shanghai Tower, consider a brief Huangpu River night cruise if you truly want to be surrounded by the spectacle.
Being on a cruise ship means you're surrounded by beautiful scenery, with ever-changing views and a stunning skyline every second. What's more, the cruise ship has a VIP area, which is perfect for those who want to avoid crowds and simply enjoy the scenery in peace.
We suggest taking the classic route, embarking from Shiliupu Marina for about 45 minutes, so you can slow-glide across the water, feel the gentle river breeze, with skyscrapers towering on both sides that no land-based viewpoint can replicate.
For more detailed information, check out: Shanghai Huangpu River Cruise: Route, Price, Tips
How to Prioritize If You Have 1, 2, or 3 Days in Shanghai
The most common mistake travelers make with a Shanghai itinerary is trying to do everything and ending up exhausted without truly experiencing anything. 
Leave your days open for discovery, and engage deeply with each experience.
Haven't decided how many days to stay in Shanghai yet? See our Shanghai Itinerary Planning Guide for your inspiration.
One Day in Shanghai: Sample the Essentials
If you only have 24 hours in Shanghai, your goal should be to feel its most dramatic contrasts in the most efficient way possible.
Morning: Explore the Former French Concession by strolling along the streets lined with leafy plane trees.
Afternoon: Admire the classical Yu Garden for its curved bridges and delicate pavilions. The bazaar outside the garden is also worth your time.
Night: Arrive at the Bund before sunset for the spectacular skyline.
This single day will give you three distinct Shanghais: the elegant, the classical, and the futuristic. All without rushing from one corner of the city to the other.
6-Day Beijing and Shanghai Tour A Tale of Two Cities 
Two Days in Shanghai: Explore by Neighbourhood
With two days, you have the luxury of slowing down and letting each area reveal itself at its own pace. The smartest strategy is to plan your time by neighbourhood, so you are not wasting valuable hours on cross-city commutes.
Explore the Huangpu District from the Bund (1 Day): Visit the old buildings along the Bund promenade, shop at Nanjing Road, wander into the Yu Garden and nearby bazaars, and return to the Bund to witness the dazzling skyline.
Feel Shanghai's Lively Side from the Former French Concession (1 Day): Stroll around the Former French Concession for the shady streets, vintage boutique stores, and tiny cafés at a leisurely pace. Jing'an Temple or Jade Buddha Temple are also optional.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
Three Days in Shanghai: Add a Day in Pudong's Future
Three days allow you to complete the time-travel experience by crossing the Huangpu River and spending a full day in Pudong, the district that represents Shanghai's tomorrow.
Observe the Future Close-Up in Pudong District (1 Day): Peak the Shanghai Tower for the panoramic view of Shanghai city, experience consumer technology at the DJI flagship store, and appreciate the sparkling Lujiazui skyline by taking the Huangpu River night cruise.
Extra Day Options: Time for a Side Trip
Wangxian Valley
If your schedule allows for a fourth day or more, or you simply want to escape the urban intensity, Shanghai offers several compelling options that reward a full day's commitment.
Zhujiajiao or Tongli Water Town: Take a boat tour to glide through its ancient canals, stone bridges, and centuries-old architecture.
Shanghai Disneyland: Perfect for families traveling with kids to enjoy themselves in Asia's biggest Disneyland.
Suzhou: Appreciate classical Chinese gardens while dressing in traditional Han costumes to travel back in time.
Hangzhou: While the West Lake is a must-see for first-timers, Hangzhou cuisine, exemplified by West Lake Fish in Vinegar Sauce, is not to be missed.
Wangxian Valley: It is more like an ancient Chinese theme park than an ancient town, but absolutely worth a night's stay for its stunning night view.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
What Is Not Worth Spending Too Much Time On in Shanghai
The fear of wasting time is one of the most common anxieties travelers bring to Shanghai: there is too much for you to see, and not everything deserves your precious hours.
Skip the over-commercialised shopping streets that you can find everywhere. Streets like Nanjing Road are not bad, but if you have limited time, unless you specifically want to buy limited-edition items at certain stores (such as the Pop Mart Global Flagship Store on Nanjing East Road), it's completely skippable.
Visiting more than one observation deck is a classic trap. Aside from the different observation deck heights, the views from the top of Shanghai Tower, Oriental Pearl Tower, and Jin Mao Tower are fundamentally the same. Choose one (preferably Shanghai Tower) and move on; the time you save can be spent in a park or a café where you will actually absorb the city's atmosphere.
Most importantly, stop trying to cover every attraction on your list. Shanghai's true value does not come from checking off landmarks. Allow yourself to pause, to look around, and let the city reveal itself at its own pace.
FAQs
Are there any unusual things to do in Shanghai besides the classical ones?
Shanghai Tian An 1000 Trees
Shanghai Tian An 1000 Trees: You won't regret coming and taking a photo here, as it features over 400 open terraces, each planted with real trees, creating a forest-like appearance that has earned it nicknames like "Shanghai's Hanging Gardens of Babylon" and the "vertical forest".
Shanghai Aurora Art Museum: Unlike the grand Shanghai Museum with its sprawling collections, the Aurora Art Museum is more private and has a stronger design personality. The museum is far less crowded, allowing you to appreciate the exhibits in peace and create a closer connection with your mind.
Shanghai People's Square: Take your time on a weekend morning, and visit a corner of People's Park that transforms into what is known as the "parental dating market". You'll see a side of Shanghai that no guidebook could ever fully capture, where Chinese parents of unmarried adults gather, bringing printed "resumes" of their children and displaying them for blind dates.
Will my kids feel bored in Shanghai? Anywhere else to visit besides Disneyland?
The Shanghai Astronomy Museum
LEGOLAND Shanghai Resort: You and your kids can easily spend 5 hours exploring this LEGOLAND theme park with an average wait time of less than 20 minutes. In contrast, without FastPass, you could wait for hours at Shanghai Disneyland.
The Shanghai Wild Animal Zoo: Great for children who love animals and outdoor exploration. It offers the rare opportunity to observe animals in more natural, open enclosures rather than cramped cages, like giant pandas and red pandas.
The Shanghai Science and Technology Museum: Excellent for curious young minds who enjoy learning about the world through hands-on play. It covers everything from robotics to human biology, and the interactive exhibits keep kids entertained for hours without feeling like schoolwork.
The Shanghai Astronomy Museum: One of the largest and most advanced astronomy museums in the world. Let your children stand on the shoulders of scientific giants and gaze into the cosmos through cutting-edge displays and immersive simulations.

Explore Shanghai with China Highlights
Before you actually set foot on Shanghai soil, what do you hope to gain from this trip?
Well, we would like to show you what we know about Shanghai: the contrast between old streets and modern towers, traditional flavors of centuries-old legacies, lively neighborhoods, and a glowing skyline by the river. 
With the right pace and route, even a short stay can reveal the many sides of this fascinating city.

 Updated May. 8, 2026 
November is one of the best months to visit Shanghai. Autumn is at its peak, offering mild, sunny days with little rainfall and noticeably fewer crowds than October.
The city averages only 5 rainy days this month, with total rainfall of about 48 mm (1.9 inches).
Daytime temperatures hover around a pleasant 17°C (62°F), perfect for outdoor exploration and city strolls. Evenings cool down quickly, dropping to around 10°C (50°F), so packing an extra layer is essential to stay comfortable.
Is November a Good Month to Visit Shanghai?
Red maple leaves on the river in Shanghai Gongqing Forest Park
Yes, November is an excellent month to visit Shanghai. 
The weather is crisp, sunny days are plentiful, and after the October Golden Week, China's major holidays are over. You can expect fewer crowds and gradually cooling prices, which is a perfect combination for a relaxed city trip.
However, November is not a single, uniform month. Based on recent weather patterns, we divide it into three distinct periods:
1. Early November (1－10): Warm, Sunny, but "Transitional" Foliage
This is your last chance to enjoy Shanghai's lingering warmth before the first winter chill arrives, which is ideal for travelers who are sensitive to cold or don't prioritize peak foliage.
Temperatures are still mild, ranging from 14－20°C (57－68°F), with plenty of sunshine. The autumn colors are just beginning, so you are more likely to see a mix of green leaves turning yellow. 
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
2. Mid-November (11－20): Cold Snap, Rain, and Rapid Color Change
Around mid-month, a cold front typically sweeps through, bringing 4－5 days of rain and a sharp temperature drop of around 8°C (46°F). 
This sudden chill accelerates the autumn colors, and you may be amazed by leaves turning vibrant red and gold almost overnight. 
However, outdoor activities become cold and damp. If your trip falls during this window, we recommend balancing your itinerary with more indoor attractions like museums, art galleries, or shopping malls to stay comfortable and dry.
3. Late November (21－30): Peak Autumn Scenery with Pleasant Days
By late November, autumn is in full glory. Temperatures stabilize at a cool 7－15°C (45－59°F), and sunny days return. 
The city's famous "no-sweeping" policy leaves fallen golden leaves lining the streets, creating postcard-worthy scenes. 
It's the perfect time to stroll through tree-lined avenues like Wukang Road of the French Concession, coffee in hand, soaking in the serene beauty of Shanghai at its most poetic.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
What to See and Do in Shanghai in November?
As a first-timer to Shanghai, beyond the Bund (admire the dazzling evening skyline) and the Shanghai Tower (the world's third tallest building), November in Shanghai offers a quieter, more poetic treasure: the autumn colors. 
This is the month when the city dresses in gold and red, inviting you to slow down and savor its seasonal beauty.
For Early Autumn Colors: Chinese Traditional Gardens
Early autumn scenery in Yu Garden, Shanghai
Yu Garden (Yuyuan) and Guyi Garden are at their most charming in early November. 
Although the autumn leaves have not yet all changed color, the first blush of red maple leaves and turning ginkgo trees have already added a lot of color to the ancient pavilions and winding corridors.
Unlike the crowded peak season, you can enjoy some serene November mornings here, which is perfect for a leisurely stroll through the Chinese traditional Jiangnan garden aesthetic.
For Golden Sycamore Strolls: The French Concession
Autumn urban road landscape in Wutong District, French Concession, Shanghai
In mid-to-late November, the tree-lined avenues of the French Concession transform into magical tunnels of golden plane tree leaves, especially around Sinan Mansions on Sinan Road. 
Walking on this thick carpet of autumn feels like stepping into a postcard. But beyond the beautiful scenery, our guide will also take you on a journey to learn about the legendary figure, Du Yuesheng. This once-powerful mob boss rose from nothing to become the "Emperor of Shanghai's Underworld."
For Vibrant Ginkgo and Local Life: Gubei Huangjincheng Avenue
For a more locally cherished autumn spot, head to Huangjincheng Avenue (Golden City Avenue) in Shanghai Changning Hongqiao Gubei Community, which is more authentic, lively, and less touristy.
Here, a dazzling avenue of ginkgo trees turns brilliant yellow, creating a canopy of sunshine. You will be welcomed by a neighborhood that buzzes with family-friendly energy, see children kicking through leaves, couples taking photos, and small shops selling warm treats. 
For Seasonal Magic: Shanghai Disneyland
November is a transitional month of pure magic at Shanghai Disneyland. 
You may still see the park decorated with a Halloween theme in Early November. By late November, the park officially launches its Christmas season, complete with giant Christmas trees, snowfall on Mickey Avenue, and festive parades. 
If you're traveling with children, this is an absolute must. The cooler weather also makes waiting in lines far more comfortable than in summer.

What to Pack and Wear in Shanghai in November
November in Shanghai means warm afternoons but chilly evenings, so layering is your best friend.
Pack a few long-sleeved shirts, a fleece or sweater, and a waterproof jacket that can handle drizzles. Jeans or comfortable trousers work fine for most days.
Don't forget a warm scarf when it becomes your best friend when the sun goes down. Comfortable, waterproof walking shoes are a must, especially if the rain appears. Sunglasses can also be useful on bright autumn days.

Shanghai Transportation
Shanghai, as the most modern international metropolis in China, has an all-round development of transportation system. No matter where you are now – overseas or in other parts of China – there are efficient and convenient transportation modes you can choose to reach Shanghai, and the diverse transportation options within the city also contribute to a worry-free Shanghai journey for you.
How to Get to Shanghai?
1. By Air – the Most Efficient Way to Arrive Shanghai from AfarSuppose your first destination in China is Shanghai, taking the plane is the most efficient way. Shanghai airports rank among the top three busiest airports in the world because of their wide coverage of airline service and dense air routes over the globe. At present, there are two airports in Shanghai – Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, with the former being the major international aviation hub whose air routes are available in more than 130 cities overseas, and the latter mainly providing flight service in Chinese mainland mostly, as well as a few short-haul routes to Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea.
By virtue of its extensive and convenient air service, Shanghai has constantly been the first stop when a large number of international tourists travel in China, as well as the transfer stop as many tourists travel to other Asian countries such as Japan and South Korea. Terminal of Shanghai Pudong International Airport  
2. By Bullet Train – More Efficient Option to Reach Shanghai within a Short-to-Medium Distance
Taking the bullet train can be a good choice if you depart from other Chinese cities to Shanghai, since 97% of Chinese cities have direct high-speed rail connections to Shanghai. In particular, if your departure location is not too far away from Shanghai, taking the high-speed train will be more cost-effective. For instance, it only takes 30 - 60 minutes to arrive Shanghai from its neighboring cities in the Yangtze River Delta including Suzhou, Hangzhou, Nanjing, etc. and 4 - 5 hours from central part of China like Beijing.
Nevertheless, the train journey from farther cities such as Xi'an and Chongqing to Shanghai takes a relatively longer time, approximately 6 hours. Therefore, if you have a tight schedule, you are more recommended to travel by air, which allows you to arrive in 2 - 2.5 hours.
Among all railway stations in the city, Shanghai Railway Station is the closest one to Shanghai downtown, followed by Shanghai South Railway Station and Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station. They all link with metro lines that can reach the Bund in 20 - 40 minutes. Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station Shanghai Bullet Trains 
 You may like:
West Railway Station 
East Railway Station 
3. By Cruise
Thanks to its advantageous location along the coast, Shanghai also has a well-developed maritime transportation system. The international cruise routes mainly include Japan, South Korea, and some Southeastern Asian countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and finally arrive at Shanghai Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal. Shanghai Cruise Shanghai Cruise on the Sea  
How to Get Around in Shanghai?
The transportation within Shanghai is efficient and travelers-friendly as well, with a diverse range of public transportation modes for you to pick. Subway, buses, and taxis all provide real-time service for you to visit various attractions and commercial districts; feature transportation like ferries, sightseeing buses, and the bund sightseeing tunnel are also available, not only facilitating your itinerary but also offering you unique experience to appreciate beautiful views of Shanghai.
1. By Metro
Taking the metro is preferred for traveling around Shanghai, especially during morning and evening peak hours on weekdays, which helps you in avoiding the traffic congestion on the roads. Besides, taking the subway is very economical, with a one-way fare ranging from CNY 3 to 26.
Currently, there are 20 metro lines in service in Shanghai. They not only connect the two airports and major railway stations, but also cover most attractions and commercial districts. For example, Shanghai Metro Line 1 links Hongqiao International Airport, Hongqiao Railway Station and the Bund; and Line 2 passes through Pudong International Airport, Shanghai Railway Station, Shanghai South Railway Station, People's Square, as well as Shanghai Tower, etc. Train Platform of Shanghai Metro Line 2 Inside Shanghai Metro Train 
  You may also want to know:
Shanghai Metro Maps
How to Take Shanghai Metro 
2. By Taxi Shanghai Taxi If you are burdened with luggage, then taking the taxi would be more comfortable, since taking the subway involves going back and forth between the station halls and the train platforms, as well as going through luggage security checks, which are inevitable. Moreover, traveling by taxi is one of the recommended modes during off-peak hours. Whether hailing a taxi by the roadside or ordering a taxi ride through the online platform, you can quickly board the vehicle and set off. Particularly if you want to visit some scenic spots in the suburbs of Shanghai, such as Zhujiajiao Water Town, whose entrance to the scenic area is about 15 minutes' walk from the nearest subway station, taking a taxi can send you directly to the destination.
The taxi fare in Shanghai is relatively reasonable. The cost for traveling between attractions within the city is approximately CNY 40 - 80 (USD 6 - 12), while the fare for going to the airport or more distant suburban attractions is about CNY 150 - 300 (USD 23 - 45). 
3. By BusThere are diverse buses in Shanghai, including City Bus, Sightseeing Bus, Tourist Bus, as well as Long-distance Bus.
City Bus: The city buses have extensive routes covering almost everywhere around Shanghai, serving as an alternative to the metro and perfectly making up for the inconvenience of some subway stations being a bit far from the entrance of certain tourist attractions. During off-peak hours, you may consider traveling by city bus, which helps you save money and also offer you convenience to admire the street views along the journey.
Sightseeing Bus: Shanghai boasts a lot of sightseeing buses, allowing you to visit the city’s landmark attractions in one go. What’s more, the buses are equipped with headphones that support multiple languages, making it easier for you to understand the history and fascinating stories behind different attractions. The most recommended sightseeing bus route is City Sightseeing Line 1, which connects the Bund, Lujiazui, Yu Garden, Nanjing Road, and People’s Square, among other core attractions. Shanghai Sightseeing Bus Shanghai Tourist Buses 
Tourist Bus: There are many tourist buses heading for scenic areas that are far away from the city center or located in some nearby cities. For instance, you can take the tourist bus from Shanghai South Railway Station directly to Shanghai Disneyland Park in 40 minutes at the cost of CNY 10, which is more time-saving and relaxing than taking the crowded metro. Besides, there are tourist buses from Shanghai Hongqiao Airport / Railway Station to Wuzhen Water Town operating four times each day, with the one-way ticket fare of CNY 55.
Long-distance Bus: If you are going to travel from Shanghai downtown to suburbs or its neighboring cities like Suzhou and Hangzhou, there are also long-distance buses for your consideration except for bullet trains.
4. By Ferry / Bund Sightseeing TunnelTaking ferry is the most cost-effective way to travel between the banks of the Huangpu River. For just CNY 2, you can get to the opposite bank in 10 minutes. As a bonus, you avoid the overcrowded entries / exits of the metro station, and gain an unforgettable experience to enjoy the fabulous river views. Additionally, if you want to visit Chongming Island, Changxing Island, or Hengsha Island near Shanghai downtown, you can also take the ferry.
The Bund Sightseeing Tunnel offers another way to travel between the two sides of the Huangpu River, providing a direct 3- to 5-minute passage to the opposite bank. As you go through the tunnel, you’ll experience fascinating visual and auditory effects that create a sensation of traveling through time and space. However, it’s somewhat more expensive, with a one-way fare of CNY 50.
5. By Shared BicycleWith pleasant weather, riding a bike to tour around Shanghai is really enjoyable, which helps you save energy and allows you to fully capture the multifarious scenery from place to place. The most recommended cycling route is the Greenway along the east bank of the Huangpu River, where you can take in the river views and landmarks of Shanghai such as the Bund Architectural Complex and the Oriental Pearl Tower. Shanghai Ferries Shanghai Shared Bicycles  
How to Pay for Public Transportation in Shanghai?
1. Using NFC PaymentIf your phone supports NFC payment, you can add your bank card such as UnionPay chip cards, Visa cards, Mastercards, American Express, and JCB contactless cards to the Wallet application such Apple Pay on your phone. Just make sure that there is sufficient balance in your card and that low-value password-free payment works, and then you can pay for metro ride by swiping NFC.
2. By CashCash is the most direct way to pay for public transportation in Shanghai. However, you are advised to prepare some change in advance since payment for the bus fee is usually in a self-help way, CNY 2 per trip. As for buying metro tickets, there are self-service ticket machines in the station halls that accept only banknotes of denominations of CNY 5, 10, and 20. You can also buy the metro ticket at the manual service counter, which is available in every metro station hall.
3. Using Shanghai Public Transportation Card Shanghai Metro Three-Day Pass You can use Shanghai Public Transportation Card in any transportation scenario, including taking the metro and bus, and even the ferry and Shanghai taxi. The card comes in two varieties, one is purple that can only be used in Shanghai, and the other is red that is valid nationwide. Both cost CNY 20 each, and can be purchased in most metro stations.
4. Using Metro Day PassOne-day Travel Pass and Three-day Travel Pass are two types of metro tickets mostly suitable for travelers. They can be purchased both at self-service ticket machines and the manual service counters in most subway stations.
The One-day Travel Pass costs CNY 18 and can be used unlimited times within 24 hours; the Three-day Travel Pass costs CNY 45 and can be used unlimited times within 72 hours. You may decide which ticket to buy based on your stay in Shanghai.
5. WeChat / Alipay QR Code ScanningIf you have a WeChat or Alipay account with proper payment functionality, you will find it much easier to use any mode of transportation. First, add the ride codes for Shanghai Metro and city buses on the WeChat Ride mini-program or in the Transport section of Alipay. Then, simply open the corresponding ride code before boarding to pay the fare. For taking taxis, you can choose to order one online in the travel service section of the ride application, or scan the driver’s QR code after arriving at your destination for payment. Top 8 Shopping Areas in Shanghai
Shanghai, famed as the “Shopping Paradise” and the “Oriental Paris”, offers an irresistible allure that makes shopping an essential and unmissable part of any visit. Be it the pursuit of high-end luxury labels, the discovery of traditional Chinese souvenirs, or the immersion in the vibrant atmosphere of local markets, this metropolis unfailingly delivers a shopping escapade that is both superlative and all-encompassing.
1. Nanjing Road - The Most Prosperous Shopping Street
Nanjing Road is one of the most bustling shopping streets in Shanghai, stretching over five kilometers in length and divided into two parts. The eastern part is dotted with specialty stores and diminutive shops that offer a wide array of clothing and electronic items. On the west side, you'll find upscale shopping malls and flagship stores of international luxury brands such as Cartier and Dior. Along this vibrant thoroughfare, numerous cafes and restaurants are conveniently situated, affording weary shoppers a welcome respite. Additionally, there are tram lines running from one end of the street to the other, providing an energy-saving way to go shopping.
More to see:  East Nanjing Road, East Nanjing Road Shopping Malls & Restaurants, West Nanjing Road Nanjing Road, Shanghai A shopping mall on Huaihai Road 
2. Huaihai Road - Luxury Goods Gathering Place
Huaihai Road, a quintessential high-end fashion shopping boulevard in Shanghai, is home to a sprawling array of over 400 stores. It serves as a magnet for a multitude of international luxury brands. Renowned names such as Gucci, Chanel, and Louis Vuitton have established their flagship emporiums here, presenting the latest and trendiest collections of clothing, bags, shoes, and other fashionable accouterments of the current season.
3. Yuyuan Bazaar - The Grand Bazaar of Traditional Features
Yuyuan Bazaar, being one of Shanghai's historical and cultural landmarks, exhibits a distinctively unique Chinese traditional style. It houses a diverse range of Chinese-style commodities and handicrafts, accompanied by numerous food stalls. Here, visitors can purchase souvenirs that are rich in Chinese characteristics, such as silk products, antiques, jade, and traditional handicrafts, thereby enabling them to immerse themselves in and experience the alluring charm of Chinese traditional culture.  Yuyuan Bazaar, Shanghai An exquisite store in Tianzifang 
4. Tianzifang - The Fusion of Art and Shopping
Tianzifang, nestled in the French Concession of Shanghai, is a charming district where many edifices preserve the architectural essence of the 1930s. Comprising a labyrinth of narrow and winding alleys, it houses a profusion of art studios, galleries, and specialty boutiques. Here, one can relish the sight of avant-garde paintings, sculptures, photographic masterpieces, and other forms of artistic expression, while also having the opportunity to acquire handicrafts, exquisite jewelry, T-shirts emblazoned with artistic motifs, and other unique commodities. Moreover, it serves as a haven for photography aficionados, as even a spontaneous click can yield a photograph replete with artistic charm.
5. Xintiandi - The Trendy Place Blending the Old and the New
Xintiandi, a remarkable blend of tradition and modernity, as well as an integration of the East and the West. The northern block preserves the time-honored Shikumen buildings, while the southern block infuses new urban vitality. Surrounding the area, prosperous edifices host a variety of establishments such as gourmet restaurants, cozy book bars, exotic cafes, and high-end shopping malls. The nightlife here is also very rich. There are many bars and entertainment venues, which are good places for you to relax and feel the vitality of modern urban Shanghai after shopping. Xintiandi, Shanghai Prcelains in the Yunzhou Curio City 
6. Yunzhou Curio City - The Treasure Hunting Spot for Antique Collections
The Yunzhou Curio City, a significant antique trading market in Shanghai, houses hundreds of stalls brimming with a diverse range of antique treasures. Within it, one can discover antique porcelain pieces hailing from various epochs and exhibiting an array of shapes. Vintage cameras are also present, bearing the photographic memories of bygone times, and old vinyl records that enable one to savor the charm of the music from years past.
7. AP Plaza – A Paradise for Budget Shoppers
The AP Plaza is renowned for its budget-friendly offerings. The stalls are densely populated with an extensive assortment of merchandise. Here, one can encounter “substitute” items of clothing in the styles of various prominent brands, sporting diverse designs that stay in tune with the latest fashion fads. Despite their lack of authenticity, the prices are highly accessible. If the genuineness of the products is not a concern for you and you place greater emphasis on cost-effectiveness and distinctive aesthetics, then exploring this market for a shopping spree will prove to be an engaging and enjoyable experience.
8. The South Bund Fabric Market - The Ideal Place for Custom-Made Clothing South Bund Fabric Market, Shanghai 
The South Bund Fabric Market stands as an optimal destination for bespoke clothing. It presents a rich selection of fabrics, such as silk, chiffon, leather, and others, which vary in both material and color. Be it an elaborate dress, a trendy suit, or a traditional Chinese cheongsam or gown, the proficient tailors here are capable of customizing it to your precise specifications. Bargaining is a common practice in this market. You can engage in price negotiation with the tailors and thereby obtain satisfactory custom-made clothing at a more economical price.
